title: Ἡμίονος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 128 (= Perry 315). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἡμίονός τις ἐκ κριθῆς παχυνθεῖσα ἀνεσκίρτησε καθ’ ἑαυτὴν βοῶσα· « Πατήρ μού ἐστιν ἵππος ὁ ταχυδρόμος, κἀγὼ δὲ αὐτῷ ὅλη ἀφωμοιώθην. »
sentences.tr: Hēmionos tis ek krithēs pachyntheisa aneskirtēse kath’ heautēn boōsa· « Patēr mou estin hippos ho tachydromos, kagō de autōi holē aphōmoiōthēn. »
sentences.l: A certain mule, fattened on barley, began to prance, crying to herself: « My father is the swift-running horse, and I too have been made wholly like him. »
sentences.n: A mule's sire is the donkey and its dam the mare; this one claims the swift-running horse for a father, and the fable turns on that. ἡμίονος is feminine here, as the participles show. κἀγώ is crasis for καὶ ἐγώ, the two words run together under one accent. ἐκ with the genitive gives the material she was fattened out of.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ ἐν μιᾷ ἀνάγκης ἐπελθούσης, ἠναγκάζετο ἡ ἡμίονος τρέχειν.
sentences.tr: Kai dē en miāi anankēs epelthousēs, ēnankazeto hē hēmionos trechein.
sentences.l: And in fact, on a certain day, a necessity having come upon her, the mule was compelled to run.
sentences.n: ἐν μιᾷ leaves ἡμέρᾳ unsaid — 'on one', that is, one day. The noun ἀνάγκη and the verb ἠναγκάζετο are the same root twice over: the necessity came, and it necessitated her.

sentences.t: Ὡς δὲ τοῦ δρόμου ἐπέπαυτο, σκυθρωπάζουσα πατρὸς τοῦ ὄνου εὐθὺς ἀνεμνήσθη.
sentences.tr: Hōs de tou dromou epepauto, skythrōpazousa patros tou onou euthys anemnēsthē.
sentences.l: But when she had ceased from the running, growing sullen, she at once remembered her father the donkey.
sentences.n: ἀναμιμνῄσκομαι takes the genitive of the thing remembered, and παύομαι the genitive of what one leaves off. σκυθρωπάζω is to wear the sour, downcast face — the word is built from σκυθρός and ὤψ, 'of gloomy countenance'.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι δεῖ, κἂν ὁ χρόνος ἐνέγκῃ τινὰ εἰς δόξαν, τῆς ἑαυτοῦ ἀρχῆς μὴ ἐπιλαθέσθαι· ἀβέβαιος γάρ ἐστιν ὁ βίος οὗτος.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti dei, kan ho chronos enenkēi tina eis doxan, tēs heautou archēs mē epilathesthai· abebaios gar estin ho bios houtos.
sentences.l: The fable shows that it is necessary, even if time should carry someone into repute, not to forget one's own beginning; for this life is unsteady.
sentences.n: κἂν is crasis for καὶ ἐάν, here concessive, 'even if'. ἀρχή is 'beginning, origin', not 'rule' — the mule's origin is the donkey. ἐπιλανθάνομαι takes the genitive of what is forgotten, and the μή belongs to the infinitive under δεῖ.
